intro: Nairobi is Kenya's capital, and on its northern edge lies Karura Forest, more than a thousand hectares of trees saved from developers in a campaign led by Wangari Maathai. A reader sent us a tree from its western part, Sigiria: three pale, mottled trunks rising together in the garden by the coffee house. We do not yet know its species or age, and we would like to.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this tree from Karura Forest, the big forest on Nairobi's northern edge, photographed after dark in the garden by the Sigiria Coffee House.

Lit from below, the tree looks carved. Three pale trunks, smooth and mottled like weathered stone, climb out of one base and lean apart, the tallest bending in a slow S before it breaks into a crown of crooked silver branches. Above them a dark canopy of small leaves fills the sky, with string lights glowing through the garden behind and a café umbrella at the edge of the frame.

We do not yet know what kind of tree it is, how old it is, or how far round the trunks are, and the reader did not say. If you know it, tell us here; a photograph of a leaf, a flower or a fruit would settle the name.

Sigiria is the western part of Karura, cut off from the rest by Limuru Road. In the 1990s much of the forest was secretly handed out for housing, and in January 1999 women led by Wangari Maathai were attacked while planting trees in protest; the campaign she led helped save it. Go in daylight and look for the pale trunks by the coffee house.

A forest of more than a thousand hectares on Nairobi's northern edge, in three parts divided by Limuru and Kiambu roads. Sigiria is its western part. A campaign led by Wangari Maathai in the late 1990s helped save it from being built on.
